analysis.one_liner: Creates federal-state partnerships to cover college costs so students can attend public college debt-free.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in June 2023 with 12 cosponsors, never advanced past its committee referral before the 118th Congress ended, and no vote was ever taken on it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a federal grant program matching each state's higher education spending, on the condition that states cover whatever college costs a student's family and existing aid leave unpaid at in-state public colleges. States would have had to freeze tuition at current levels, keep funding public higher education, and reach every eligible student within five years. It also would have sent grants to historically Black colleges and minority-serving institutions to cover their students' unmet costs, and made Dreamer students brought to the U.S. as children eligible for federal financial aid.
analysis.who_benefits: Students at in-state public colleges who would have had their remaining tuition and living-cost gap covered, starting with Pell Grant recipients; HBCUs, tribal colleges, and other minority-serving institutions and their students, who would have received dedicated grants; and Dreamer students, who would have become eligible for federal financial aid. Students would graduate without college loans.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public college students and their families

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Education Department to award states grants covering unmet financial need — the gap between a student's cost of attendance and what they and existing grant aid can pay — for every eligible student at in-state public colleges, with Pell Grant recipients covered first.
Requires participating states to cap public college tuition and fees at 2023 levels (with only inflation-based increases), so tuition could not rise to absorb the aid.
Requires states to maintain or increase their own higher education funding as a condition of receiving federal money, and to submit and meet a five-year plan approved by the Education Department.

Creates a parallel grant program for HBCUs, tribal colleges, and other minority-serving institutions to cover their students' unmet need, with tuition caps and maintenance-of-effort conditions attached.
Extends federal student aid eligibility to Dreamer students who entered the U.S. before age 16 and completed high school, college coursework, or military service.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through a new authorization of $84 billion for the first year and 'such sums as may be necessary' through 2033, plus $3 billion for the HBCU and minority-serving institution program. States would also have had to keep paying at least their recent funding levels as their share of the partnership.

drawbacks.text: The program is expensive: it authorizes $84 billion for fiscal year 2024 alone, plus whatever sums are 'necessary' through 2033, a major new federal obligation on top of existing aid programs.

Because each state's grant equals its entire annual higher education operating support, the design roughly doubles public higher education funding from combined federal and state sources, which critics would call a large federalization of a state responsibility; the bill's maintenance-of-effort rules protect against states cutting their own spending but do not reduce the total cost.
Tuition caps tied to the Consumer Price Index could squeeze college operating budgets in years when their costs rise faster than inflation, potentially forcing trade-offs in program quality.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — eliminating college debt for students at public institutions, weighted toward low-income students — is large and concrete, and the bill builds in real guardrails: tuition caps, state maintenance-of-effort rules, oversight with probation and ineligibility for breaching states, and protections so enrolled students keep coverage even if a state withdraws. The cost is genuinely large: a new federal spending stream on the scale of tens of billions per year, on top of existing grant and loan programs. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how one weighs debt relief and college access against federal budget priorities; the bill's design addressed the most common failure mode of such programs (states using federal money to replace, rather than add to, their own spending).

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Pocan introduced the Debt-Free College Act of 2023 in the House on June 7, 2023, joined by nine other representatives as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day; that referral is the last action in its history.
Twelve House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it, and the House committee, controlled by the Republican majority, never held a markup or brought it to the floor.
No vote was ever taken in either chamber before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of expanding federal spending on higher education — effectively, the House Republican majority that controlled the committee — got the outcome they preferred at no cost, since the bill never even reached a committee vote. The status quo of student debt and state-level college funding arrangements continued unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The House majority that never acted on it

for.name: Rep. Mark Pocan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited nine original cosponsors on the day of introduction.

for.name: 12 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none of them chaired a committee that could advance it.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, held by the House Republican majority
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 7, 2023 and took no further action on it — no markup, no vote, no report — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the House committee agenda
against.what_they_did: Supported no cosponsors and allowed the bill to sit without committee action until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All ten original sponsors and all twelve later cosponsors were House Democrats; the bill drew no Republican support and never left the Republican-controlled committee [S3][S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have roughly doubled combined federal-state operating support for public institutions, funded student success programs (4% of state grants), and allowed up to 5% for capacity like faculty hiring and facilities. In return, institutions would have faced tuition caps and reporting requirements.

A debt-free guarantee at public colleges, with states barred from counting private loans against a student's need, would have reduced demand for student borrowing. The bill died, so the existing lending market continues unchanged.

A separate $3 billion annual authorization would have covered unmet need for their students, with tuition caps and enrollment-maintenance conditions. Most private nonprofit HBCUs and minority-serving institutions would have qualified; recently converted for-profits were excluded.

For-profit institutions were excluded from the HBCU/MSI grant program, and for-profits that converted to nonprofit status within 25 years were specifically barred — provisions aimed at keeping the new aid out of the for-profit sector.
